first.rationale: Two of the three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are directly addressed by the onboarding/signup friction lever, and that lever plausibly compounds into retained, non-discounted revenue — which matches the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Promotional pricing (memory_73) is the tempting reactive answer to the competitor, but its recorded win was an acquisition/revenue-lift result, not a durable-value result; discount-led SMB acquisition risks importing exactly the price-sensitive cohort the competitor is courting and depressing long-run qualified revenue, so I am declining it this slot. Referral incentive (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) are both credible but address neither of the two measured declines this quarter. Activation messaging (memory_91) treats the symptom downstream of the funnel step that is itself degrading; fixing onboarding first is the better-ordered intervention. I am spending both verification pulls on the memories my chosen action actually rests on rather than on the option I am rejecting: memory_86 (shortening onboarding) is the direct load-bearing claim, and memory_31 (cutting required signup fields) is both older (day 12) and the mechanism I would most likely implement. Key downstream risk to instrument: removing required signup fields strips qualification data, which can silently degrade the demo-request/sales-assist pipeline quality that memory_44 depends on — so an activation lift could be bought with worse enterprise lead quality. I will therefore run this as a controlled experiment with a holdout and measure not just completion/activation but downstream qualified-pipeline and 30/90-day retained revenue, and I will not treat the inherited lifts as guaranteed to reproduce: they are archived, aged, and were measured before the current competitive shift, which may itself be the cause of the declines rather than any funnel regression.

mid.rationale: Verification sharpened rather than changed the call, and it changed the mechanism. exp_86 is the stronger record: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and crucially 30-day retention +3% — a lift that shows up in retained value, not just top-of-funnel. exp_31 is weaker than its summary implied: the lift is real but SMB-only, explicitly not replicated on other segments, and it carries 30-day retention -1% against qualified revenue +4%. That negative retention signal is exactly the downstream cost the consolidated memory line ('a durable lift in first-week activation') had rounded away. So I commit to simplify_onboarding via the exp_86 mechanism — shortening and resequencing the post-signup flow — and I explicitly do NOT strip required signup fields. That choice preserves the qualification data the demo-request/sales-assist path (memory_44) depends on, avoiding the failure mode where an activation win is silently paid for with worse enterprise pipeline quality. This directly targets both measured declines: onboarding completion -4% and activation -6%, with activation partly downstream of the onboarding step itself. I continue to decline promotional_pricing (memory_73) despite it being the reflexive answer to the competitor's entry pricing: its recorded result is acquisition and revenue lift, not durable value, and discount-led acquisition of the same price-sensitive SMB cohort the competitor is courting is the most likely way to book short-term revenue that does not survive renewal — a poor trade against a 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' objective. referral_incentive (memory_57) and enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) address neither declining metric this quarter. Standard experiment, not broad rollout: all these records are archived and aged (day 52 and earlier), measured before the current competitive shift, and the declines may be driven by mix change from competitor-driven churn rather than by any funnel regression — in which case a funnel fix will underperform its historical effect size. Instrument accordingly: holdout control, primary on completion and week-one activation, guardrails on 30/90-day retained revenue, qualified-pipeline volume and lead quality by segment, and segment splits so an SMB-only effect is not mistaken for a general one. If guardrails hold, scale next cycle; if pipeline quality degrades, roll back rather than iterate.

final2.rationale: Holding the decision. The new information is genuinely bad news but it is not evidence that changes which lever produces sustainable qualified revenue — it raises the price of not reacting, which is a different thing. The one record I verified that speaks to durable value is exp_86: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%. That is the only lever in the set with a confirmed retention-positive result. The pricing lever (memory_73) remains unverified consolidated summary text, and what it claims is acquisition and revenue lift, not durability. Matching a competitor who has now cut twice in one week means bidding against an opponent who has shown he will cut again; winning that auction retains the most price-sensitive cohort at a permanently lower price point, which is close to the worst available trade against a long-term qualified-revenue objective. If the competitor's price is genuinely below our sustainable floor, those accounts are not defensible with the experiment slot and discounting mostly converts churn into margin loss. I also note the specific trap: exp_31's SMB signup-simplification result showed 30-day retention -1%, so the SMB-targeted variant of my own lever is the one with a retention cost. I stay with the exp_86 mechanism — shorten and resequence post-signup onboarding, do not strip required signup fields — which protects the qualification data the sales-assist path (memory_44) needs and does not chase the fleeing price-sensitive segment. Separately and outside this slot: the doubled churn conversations are a retention-operations problem, not an experiment. Targeted save conversations, case-by-case commercial discretion for high-value accounts, and honest value framing can run today without consuming the experiment slot, and leadership should get that as the immediate response rather than a blanket price move. Uncertainty I am explicitly carrying: the competitor shock is now actively changing the customer mix, so the -6% activation and -4% completion declines may be partly composition effects rather than funnel regression, and exp_86's historical effect size may not reproduce under the new mix. Run with a holdout, segment splits, and guardrails on 30/90-day retained revenue and qualified-pipeline quality; read the result as directional, not as confirmation. If retained revenue in the SMB base keeps deteriorating after this cycle, the right escalation is a deliberate segment and pricing-floor decision made with fresh evidence next week — not a reflexive match today.
